guide.title: Vital Signs
guide.lead: One set of vital signs is a snapshot; the trend is the story. Know the normal ranges for each age, measure carefully with the right equipment, and repeat often. A falling BP and a rising pulse matter more than any single number.

sections.title: Normal at rest (awake)
notes: SpO₂ 94–98% on room air; temperature about 37 °C (fever 38 °C or more); capillary refill 2 seconds or less.
Hypotension in children: systolic below 70 mmHg (infants), below 70 + (2 × age in years) for ages 1–10, below 90 mmHg from 10 years.

groups.title: BP cuff
items: Bladder about 40% of arm circumference wide and 80% long
Too small reads falsely high; too large reads falsely low

groups.title: Pulse sites
items: Unresponsive adult or child: carotid (femoral also)

groups.title: Postural (orthostatic) change
items: Systolic falls 20 mmHg or more, or diastolic 10 mmHg or more, within 3 minutes of standing
Pulse rise of 30/min or more suggests significant volume loss

quiz.q: Commonest cause of a falsely high BP reading:
options: A cuff that is too small
A cuff that is too large
quiz.explanation: Bladder about 40% of the arm circumference wide.

quiz.q: A 6-month-old has a heart rate of 150. You should:
options: Recognise it as normal for an infant and assess the rest

quiz.q: Trauma: BP 118/72, HR 96, then 15 minutes later BP 96/62, HR 122, cool and clammy. Trend?
options: Compensated shock moving to decompensation: act now

quiz.q: Pulse to check in an infant:
quiz.explanation: On the inside of the upper arm.

quiz.q: How often should an unstable patient's vital signs be rechecked?
On standing, systolic falls from 112 to 84 and pulse rises from 88 to 122. This is:
options: A significant postural drop suggesting volume loss
quiz.explanation: Systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more, pulse rise of 30/min or more.

flashcards.question: Normal breathing rates by age
flashcards.answer: Adult 12–20; adolescent 12–20; school age 18–25; preschool 20–28; toddler 22–37; infant 30–53/min.

flashcards.question: Pulse for an unresponsive adult
flashcards.answer: Carotid: beside the trachea, inside the sternocleidomastoid.

flashcards.question: Pulse for an infant
flashcards.answer: Brachial: inside of the upper arm.

flashcards.question: Cuff too small
flashcards.answer: Falsely high BP. The bladder should be about 40% of arm circumference wide and 80% long.

flashcards.question: Recheck frequency
flashcards.answer: Every 5 minutes if unstable, every 15 minutes if stable, and after every intervention.

flashcards.question: Normal SpO₂
flashcards.answer: 94–98% on room air for most people.

flashcards.question: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension
flashcards.answer: Systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more, or diastolic 10 mmHg or more, within 3 minutes of standing. A pulse rise of 30/min or more suggests significant volume loss.

critical.scenario: A 72-year-old felt dizzy on standing. Seated: HR 88, BP 112/70. On standing he goes pale: HR 122, BP 84/56. You sit him back down.
critical.question: What do the trends mean?

options.t: A significant postural drop: likely volume depletion; transport for assessment and fluids
Heart attack: aspirin and emergency transport
options.f: The pattern points to volume loss; look for bleeding (melena) too.
A 28 mmHg fall and 34/min rise is not normal.

options.t: Make him stand again to confirm

critical.explanation: Systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more, pulse rise of 30/min or more. Ask about bleeding, diuretics, vomiting and diarrhea.

critical.scenario: A 5-year-old has had fever and vomiting for 24 hours: lethargic, dry mouth, no urine for 8 hours. HR 148, BP 82/58, capillary refill 4 seconds, temperature 39.1 °C.
critical.question: Interpretation and next action?

options.t: Shock from dehydration (tachycardia, slow refill, lethargy); BP still just above the limit: oxygen, keep warm, rapid transport, fluids per protocol
Fever only: cool and routine transport
options.f: Lethargy and slow refill mean shock.

options.t: Normal for a child with fever

critical.explanation: Her limit is 70 + (2 × 5) = 80 mmHg. Children compensate until they suddenly don't.

critical.scenario: High-speed crash: confused, cool and clammy. HR 128, BP 104/70, RR 24, SpO₂ 94%. Eight minutes later: HR 136, BP 86/56, RR 28, SpO₂ 91%. 12 minutes to the trauma centre.
critical.question: Interpretation and action?

options.t: Decompensated shock: oxygen to target, vital signs every 5 minutes, ALS intercept, pre-alert, lights and sirens

critical.explanation: Falling BP with rising pulse means compensation is failing.
